To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of antisites is essential to induce visible light induced persistent photoluminescence in Cr3+ doped spinels.

(i) the presence of antisites defects in Cr3+ doped spinel AB2O4 (A = Mg or Zn, B = Al or Ga) is a necessary condition for the persistent luminescent properties of these compounds; (ii) the presence of these defects in the close environment to Cr3+ is a necessary condition to obtain a visible light induced persistent photoluminescence.

Cr(3+) doping of AB2O4 (A = Zn, Mg, B = Ga, or Al) spinels results in a persistent luminescence, which can be induced by visible-light excitation of Cr(3) centers, and that the efficiency of this process increases with increasing antisite disorder, which can be tuned by the choice of A and B elements in the AB2O4 formula.

antisite defects are necessary but not sufficient to obtain persistent luminescence, as the latter also depends on the local environment around Cr(3+) as well as on the crystal field splitting of the d-electron energy levels.

the presence of antisites in the close environment around Cr(3+) is essential for the occurrence of the visible light induced PL in AB2O4 compounds, and the PL efficiency is directly proportional to the number of antisite defects.
the presence of antisites in the spinel structure is a necessary condition, but is not sufficient, for the occurrence of the visible light induced luminescence in the Cr(3+):AB2O4 system.

the antisite disorder in ZnGa2-O4 and MgGa-2O4 is responsible for the visible light induced long persistent luminescence, while the crystal field energy is the main factor determining the efficiency of persistent luminescent emission.
